Wales. A constituent country of the United Kingdom occupying the western peninsula of Great Britain, known for its rugged mountains, castles, and distinctive Celtic culture. Conquered and formally annexed by England in fifteen thirty-six, Wales nevertheless retained a strong Welsh-language tradition and cultural identity that survived centuries of assimilation pressure. Today Wales represents a unique blend of British governance and Celtic pride, with a devolved government and a living native language.

Wales is mountainous terrain dominated by the Snowdonian Alps in the north. This geographic isolation from England fostered separate cultural development throughout medieval history. The Welsh language, Cymraeg, is a Celtic language closely related to Cornish and Breton, quite distinct from English, and it has been actively revived in recent decades. Castles are ubiquitous throughout Wales. Edward the First of England built a ring of conquest castles—Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech—after subjugating Wales in twelve eighty-two.

Wales was formally united with England under Henry the Eighth's Laws in Wales Acts, passed in fifteen thirty-six and fifteen forty-three, ending its independence but not its cultural distinctiveness. During the Industrial Revolution, South Wales became a coal-mining and steel-producing powerhouse in the nineteenth century, driving urbanization and global influence. Wales has a strong connection to Arthurian legend, with many Welsh place names and myths associating Wales with King Arthur and the Celts' mythological past. The Welsh National Eisteddfod is an annual cultural festival celebrating Welsh language, music, and literature—a living continuation of medieval bardic traditions.

Wales gained devolution in nineteen ninety-nine, acquiring its own Assembly, later called the Senedd, allowing home rule in education, health, and culture while remaining part of the United Kingdom.
